title: Find a mentor, be a mentor: the two-way gift
description: A mentor is not a guru — just someone a few steps further along the same road, willing to say where the potholes are. How to find one without awkwardness, and why offering to be one is the other half of the gift.

body.heading: Ask smaller than you fear
paragraphs: Most mentor relationships never begin because the ask feels enormous: 'Will you be my mentor?' sounds like a marriage proposal. Shrink it. Ask one specific question of someone whose work you admire, thank them properly for the answer, and let a second question follow in a month if the first went well. Mentorships grow; they are rarely declared.
Choose someone a few steps ahead, not a legend. The person who solved your exact problem last year remembers the confusion in a way the person who solved it thirty years ago may not.

body.heading: Be the kind of mentee people help twice
paragraphs: Do the homework before you ask, report back on what happened after you take advice, and never make your mentor chase you for the outcome. People happily help someone whose progress they get to witness; they quietly stop helping someone whose questions vanish into a void.
And respect the boundary of the gift: your mentor owes you honesty, not availability. Their time is the generosity — treat it that way.

body.heading: The other half: be one
paragraphs: You do not need grey hair to mentor; you need one road you have already walked. The new starter at work, the neighbour beginning the hobby you know, the cousin facing the exam you passed — each is waiting for exactly the map in your head.
Offering costs little and pays strangely well: explaining what you know reveals what you only thought you knew. Find a mentor, be a mentor, and you have joined the oldest education system there is.

takeaway: Ask one small question, report back on the result, and pass your own map on to someone behind you — mentorship is a chain, not a ceremony.
